description:
Hey there! 

We are a group of young technology enthusiasts hoping to impact communities through useful solutions. Our team, StarDrift, works on a tool that will help people to study star movements from their web browser. We want people to discover the sky regardless of their background in astronomy.
summary:
Star Drift is a web app for exploring NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey, built to help people find faint and moving sources that fixed images hide. Existing citizen-science tools like Backyard Worlds show pre-rendered PNGs. You can’t change the field of view, compare epochs, or see what a source looks like across SPHEREx’s 102 spectral bands.

Star Drift addresses the SphereX/PlanetX challenge by treating the search for distant, slow-moving objects as an image-comparison problem. A user enters coordinates and a field of view, then blinks or differences images from different epochs. Moving sources show up as changes between epochs, and Gaia, WISE and SIMBAD overlays help rule out known stars and galaxies. It matters because SPHEREx will keep releasing data, and a tool that updates easily and gives researchers and volunteers real analysis tools, not just pictures, makes candidate discovery faster and more reliable.
details:
What it does

  • Loads SPHEREx sky images for any coordinates and field of view, set by the user or by URL query so views can be shared and embedded.
  • Blinks and differences images across epochs to reveal motion.
  • Lets users move through the 102 infrared bands with a slider, view per-detector coadds, and generate spectra on the fly.
  • Overlays Gaia, WISE and SIMBAD sources with labels, and shows metadata such as contamination flags.
  • Uses clean stretching and rendering so images don’t look noisy or unfinished.

How it works

  • Data engine: ingests SPHEREx releases and processes them with Astropy into tiles and metadata.
  • Database: PostGIS for spatial queries by sky position.
  • Rendering: a WebGL engine for fast, client-side display, stretching, blinking and subtraction.
  • Frontend: React with Vite.
  • Aladin tools are used for catalog overlays and sky context.

Benefits: it updates easily as new SPHEREx releases arrive; it works interactively without downloading raw data; it gives vetting context (known catalog sources, contamination flags) in one place; and it can be embedded elsewhere through URL parameters.

What we hope to achieve: a practical tool that lowers the barrier to finding candidate sources in SPHEREx data, with a path to add free-form band math and automated ingestion later.

Tools and technologies: Python, Astropy, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, WebGL, JavaScript, React, Vite, Aladin Lite. The team has three full-stack developers, working on Linux and Windows.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) Tools

We used Claude (Anthropic) to help draft the design document, define requirements and phased scope, organize the work into development tickets, and review architecture decisions. All code was written and tested by our team.

NASA Data and Resources Used

  • SPHEREx mission data (all-sky spectral images in 102 infrared bands), the core dataset, accessed through IRSA.
  • WISE infrared catalog and imagery data, used for overlays.
  • Gaia catalog (ESA, a Space Agency Partner resource), used for stellar overlays and labels.
  • SIMBAD (CDS), used for object labelling.
  • Aladin / Aladin Lite (CDS), used for sky context and catalog overlays.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Data at NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA)
